title: Google just mass-fired 12,000 people and then posted a job listing for a 'Chief Happiness Officer.' I am not making this up.
content:
I genuinely thought this was satire when someone on my team Slacked it to me. Google lays off 12,000 people — via EMAIL, mind you, not even a call — and then the SAME WEEK posts a role for a Chief Happiness Officer with a compensation band of $350-450K. The job description literally includes 'fostering a culture of psychological safety and belonging.' BELONGING. For the people who still have badge access, I guess.

But here's the part that actually broke me. They removed the free kombucha from the microkitchens on the same day they announced the layoffs. The kombucha. That's like burning down your house and also canceling the newspaper subscription. It's not even a cost-saving measure at that point, it's performance art.

Meanwhile Sundar's total comp last year was $226 MILLION. You know what $226 million buys? Roughly 2,260 engineers at $100K each. But no, we needed that money for... checks notes... a CEO who sends emails titled 'A difficult decision' while sitting on a yacht that has a smaller yacht inside it.

My favorite part is the Googlers who are STILL defending this. 'Oh but the severance package is generous.' Brother, they gave people 16 weeks and then blacklisted their badge before they could even grab their desk plant. Karen from People Ops sent a follow-up email about returning your Chromebook with a smiley face emoji. A SMILEY FACE.

The tech industry isn't a meritocracy. It's a cargo cult where we worship ping pong tables and pretend stock refreshers are a personality trait. The Chief Happiness Officer position is still open btw. I'm sure they'll find someone great right after they finish escorting the last batch of laid-off employees past the nap pods.
source_title: Google's $400K 'Chief Happiness Officer' Posting Days After 12K Layoffs Sparks Outcry

title: I've been a software engineer for 20 years. The mass layoffs aren't about the economy. They're about shareholders finally realizing engineers aren't magic.
content:
I started coding professionally in 2006. I've survived three recessions, two dot-com aftershocks, and the mass delusion that was the blockchain hiring spree of 2017. What's happening now isn't a downturn. It's a CORRECTION, and frankly it's been coming for a while.

Here's what actually happened. From 2020 to 2022, interest rates were basically zero. Money was free. VCs were throwing cash at anything with a landing page and a Notion doc. And Big Tech? They went on the most absurd hiring binge in the history of capitalism. Google hired 60,000 people in two years. META hired so many people that new engineers would show up on their first day and literally have no team to join. They called it 'resting and vesting.' That was an ACTUAL TERM people used WITH A STRAIGHT FACE.

We hired 400 people to build a feature that 3 people could have shipped. The 3 people who could have shipped it spent 18 months in alignment meetings with the other 397. I personally attended a meeting about scheduling a meeting to discuss the roadmap for a planning meeting. That is not a joke. I have the calendar invite.

The dirty secret is that most of those hires weren't about building things. They were about DENYING TALENT TO COMPETITORS. It was a Cold War strategy applied to software engineers. 'If we hire all the good React developers, our competitors can't.' Except they hired a LOT of not-good React developers too and nobody noticed because everyone was too busy writing their 'impact statements' for perf review.

Now rates are up, growth is slowing, and some finance person at every major tech company finally opened a spreadsheet and said 'wait, we have 14 people on the Developer Experience for Internal Tools Platform Infrastructure team and none of them can explain what they do?' SHOCKED PIKACHU FACE.

I feel for everyone who got laid off. I really do. But I also watched a 24-year-old with 8 months of experience turn down a $400K offer because it didn't include enough equity refreshers. The market was broken. This is it unbreaking. It just sucks that the people paying the price aren't the executives who created the problem in the first place.
source_title: Tech layoffs expose decade-long myth that engineers were irreplaceable

title: Apple just announced a product that already exists, called it revolutionary, and the stock went up 4%. I love this timeline.
content:
I just sat through the entire WWDC keynote and I need someone to explain to me how a room full of adults gasped — AUDIBLY GASPED — when Apple announced split-screen multitasking on iPad. Samsung has had this since 2013. That's not a typo. Two thousand and thirteen. The feature is old enough to be in middle school.

But here's the Apple magic. They didn't call it split-screen. They called it 'Fluid Spatial Multitasking' and showed a 4-minute animation of windows gracefully gliding across the screen while a woman in a tastefully lit loft apartment pretended to be productive. And you know what? The stock went up 4%. Four percent. That's roughly $100 billion in market cap because they discovered what Android did during the Obama administration.

The real MVP of every Apple keynote is Craig Federighi. This man's hair deserves its own segment. It deserves its own KEYNOTE. He walks out there with that silver mane flowing like he just stepped off a shampoo commercial and the crowd goes nuts. He could announce that iOS is removing the phone app and people would clap. 'We think you're going to love it.'

My personal favorite moment was when they announced RCS support and framed it as Apple being generous and caring about interoperability. Brother, the EU literally FORCED you to do this. That's like a bank robber returning the money and calling himself a philanthropist. Tim Cook stood there with his hands clasped like a benevolent monk and said 'we believe in connecting everyone' as if they hadn't spent a decade deliberately making green bubble texts look like garbage to shame Android users into switching.

Also they showed a demo of an AI feature that hallucinated wrong information DURING THE KEYNOTE and nobody on stage acknowledged it. The presenter just smiled and moved on. Confidence level: sociopathic. I respect it.

I'm still going to buy everything they announced. I'm part of the problem. We all are. See you at the Apple Store on launch day, you beautiful sheep.

title: My startup raised $50M at a $500M valuation. We have 6 customers and one of them is my mom. AMA.
content:
Before you ask: yes, my mom pays full price. She's actually our highest-engagement user. She logs in every day and leaves comments like 'great job sweetie!' on the dashboard. Our investor deck lists her as a 'power user in the 55+ demographic.'

Here's how we did it. Step one: put 'AI-powered' on every single slide. Our pitch deck says AI-powered 14 times. Our AI is an if-else statement and a call to the OpenAI API with temperature set to 0.7. One of our 'proprietary models' is literally a regex. The VCs LOVED it. One partner at Andreessen told me our 'AI moat' was the strongest he'd seen all quarter. Our moat is an API key.

Step two: metrics gymnastics. We don't say 'users,' we say 'activated accounts.' We don't say 'revenue,' we say 'ARR trajectory based on contracted intent.' One of our 6 customers signed a letter of intent that is, legally speaking, worth nothing. We count it as $2M in pipeline. Our CFO — who is also me — calls this 'forward-looking accounting.' My actual accountant calls it 'concerning.'

Step three: buzzword bingo. Our product is a 'vertically-integrated, AI-native, API-first platform enabling enterprise-grade workflow orchestration for cross-functional stakeholder alignment.' It's a to-do list app. It has checkboxes. The checkboxes are nice though, they have a satisfying little animation when you click them. That animation cost $4M in engineering time.

The fundraise itself was a fever dream. We did a roadshow where I pitched 47 VCs in two weeks. I wore the same Patagonia vest to every meeting because someone told me it 'signals operator energy.' Three firms got into a bidding war over our round. None of them asked to see the product. NOT ONE. One partner told me, 'We invest in founders, not products.' Sir, the founder is a 32-year-old whose last startup was a Slack bot that nobody used.

We're using the $50M to hire 80 engineers, open an office in San Francisco that we'll use three days a week, and build an AI feature that does what our product already does but 'with intelligence.' Our burn rate is $1.2M per month. At this rate, we have roughly 41 months of runway, which I'm told is 'efficient' because at least we're not spending $3M a month like the OTHER to-do list startup that raised $120M.

Anyway, we're hiring. DM me if you want equity in a company that will either be worth $2 billion or absolutely nothing. There is no in-between.

title: Amazon just patented a method for making employees cry more efficiently. Wait, sorry, it's 'optimizing workforce emotional throughput.' My mistake.
content:
Every few months Amazon files a patent that reads like the opening chapter of a dystopian novel, and every few months I think 'surely THIS is the one that makes people care.' It never is. We just collectively shrug and order more paper towels with same-day delivery.

This latest one is a system for 'real-time cognitive load assessment in fulfillment environments.' In human language, that means sensors that monitor how stressed warehouse workers are and then ADJUST THEIR WORKLOAD to keep them at peak productivity. Not to reduce stress, mind you. To keep them at the OPTIMAL level of stress. They literally want to find the sweet spot between 'productive anxiety' and 'breakdown.' They want to ride that line like it's a surfboard.

But this isn't even the wildest one. They already have a patent for a wristband that tracks your hand movements in the warehouse and vibrates when you're reaching for the wrong item. Think about that. You're picking items for 10 hours a day and every time your hand goes the wrong direction, your wrist BUZZES at you like a shock collar for a golden retriever. But sure, the banana stand in the lobby totally makes up for it.

My personal favorite is the patent for the cage. Yes, the CAGE. They patented a human-sized cage that sits on top of a robot so workers can safely operate inside an automated warehouse floor. When the internet freaked out, Amazon said they would 'never use it.' Then WHY DID YOU PATENT IT, JEFF? You don't patent things for fun. Nobody at the patent office is doing it ironically.

I worked at an Amazon fulfillment center for 11 months. The bathroom breaks were timed. Not officially, but your rate dropped and your manager would come find you with a printout — an ACTUAL PAPER PRINTOUT — showing your items-per-hour dipping below target. One guy on my shift got written up because he took too long walking to the bathroom. His solution was to stop drinking water during shifts. Management considered this a success.

The Leadership Principles are posted on every wall like the Ten Commandments. 'Bias for Action.' 'Insist on the Highest Standards.' 'Frugality.' You know what frugality means at Amazon? It means the break room has a vending machine that only takes exact change and the microwave has been broken since 2019. But Andy Jassy's office probably has a sous chef.

Anyway I just ordered a new Kindle from Amazon because the irony of my existence is not lost on me. It'll arrive tomorrow because someone in a warehouse is being vibrated at by their wristband right now to make sure it does.
source_title: Amazon Patent Filing Signals Push Into Worker Biometric Optimization

title: Every SaaS product I use has added an AI chatbot that doesn't work. I now have 47 non-functional chatbots across my tool stack.
content:
I'm a product manager at a mid-size company and I just did an audit of every tool in our stack that has bolted on an AI chatbot in the last 18 months. The count is FORTY SEVEN. Forty seven chatbots. Not a single one of them can answer a basic question about the product it's embedded in.

I asked Jira's AI assistant to find my open tickets and it gave me a motivational quote about productivity. Thanks Jira. Very helpful. I asked Salesforce's Einstein GPT to summarize a deal pipeline and it returned a paragraph about how AI is transforming the future of CRM. That's literally Salesforce's marketing copy. It pasted its own marketing copy at me.

Slack's AI tried to summarize a channel and told me the team was 'discussing project deliverables and next steps.' EVERY CHANNEL IS DISCUSSING DELIVERABLES AND NEXT STEPS. THAT'S WHAT WORK IS. I wanted to know WHICH deliverables. WHICH next steps.

HubSpot's chatbot told me to 'check the knowledge base' when I asked it a question. YOU ARE THE KNOWLEDGE BASE. You are literally sitting on top of the knowledge base like a dragon sitting on gold except the dragon is illiterate.

Notion's AI rewrote my meeting notes in a 'more professional tone' and removed all the action items. Confluence's AI assistant generated a summary of a page that was longer than the original page. Figma's AI suggested I 'try using frames' when I asked how to export a prototype. I've been using Figma for six years.

The pattern is always the same: (1) company raises a round or needs to justify valuation (2) they add a chat bubble in the bottom right corner (3) they connect it to GPT-3.5 with zero fine-tuning and a system prompt that says 'you are a helpful assistant for [PRODUCT NAME]' (4) they write a blog post called 'Introducing [PRODUCT] AI: The Future of [CATEGORY]' (5) it doesn't work (6) nobody removes it because removing it would be admitting it doesn't work.

My favorite part is when the chatbot confidently makes up a feature that doesn't exist. I asked Zendesk's bot how to set up a specific automation and it gave me a detailed 8-step walkthrough for a settings page THAT DOES NOT EXIST IN THE PRODUCT. I followed the steps and got lost at step 2 because the menu it referenced hasn't existed since 2019.

I now mass-close every 'Have you tried our new AI assistant?' popup like I'm playing whack-a-mole. I spend more time dismissing AI chatbots than I save from any of them. The net productivity impact of the entire SaaS AI chatbot movement on my life is deeply negative.

The worst part? Every single one of these companies is now calling themselves an 'AI-first platform' in their investor updates. Brother, you are a CRUD app with a chat bubble. You are not AI-first. You are AI-adjacent at best. You are AI-curious. Stop it.
source_title: The AI Chatbot Glut: Companies Report Dozens of Nonfunctional Assistants in Software Stacks

title: Elon bought Twitter for $44 billion and turned it into a $12 billion company. That's negative $32 billion in value creation. The man is a reverse alchemist.
content:
I need someone to walk me through the timeline of this because every time I think about it I lose a year off my life.

2022: Elon Musk, the richest man on Earth, posts a Twitter poll asking if he should buy Twitter. The internet says yes because the internet always says yes to chaos. He offers $44 billion. Twitter's board says sure. He tries to back out. He gets sued. He buys it anyway. He walks into the office carrying a SINK because he thinks he's funny.

Week one: Fires 80% of the staff including the entire trust and safety team, most of the infrastructure engineers, and the communications department. Tweets 'the bird is freed.' Freed from what? From functioning?

Week two: Verification system is now $8/month. Anyone can get a blue check. Someone immediately impersonates Eli Lilly and tweets that insulin is free. Eli Lilly's stock drops. The pharmaceutical industry discovers what shitposting is.

Month two: Fires the trust and safety team and then is shocked — SHOCKED — when advertisers left. My brother in Christ, Coca-Cola doesn't want their ad next to a guy named @TruthPatriot1488. That's not woke. That's just brand management. That's literally day one of advertising school. 'Don't put the product next to the extremism' is not a controversial position.

Month six: Renames the entire platform to X. Nobody calls it X. Your grandmother still calls it Twitter. Journalists still call it Twitter. The app icon looks like it was designed in Microsoft Paint at 2am which, knowing the remaining engineering team's work schedule, it probably was.

Year one: Revenue down 50%+. Fidelity marks down its equity stake repeatedly. The company that was purchased for $44 billion is now valued at roughly $12 billion. That's not a loss. That's a MAGIC TRICK. Making $32 billion in value disappear should be studied in business schools the way they study Enron.

Year two: He's posting through it. He's posting memes. He's posting ALL DAY. The CEO of Tesla, SpaceX, and whatever Neuralink is supposed to be is spending 14 hours a day getting into reply wars with accounts that have 47 followers. The man has rockets going to Mars and he's arguing about PRONOUNS with an egg avatar.

The funniest part to me is the people who say 'well he's playing 4D chess, you just don't understand the strategy.' THE STRATEGY IS LOSING $32 BILLION. If that's chess then I've been playing chess wrong my entire life.

Someone in the replies is going to tell me X is actually doing great and I should look at the engagement metrics. My brother, a dumpster fire also has great engagement metrics. Everyone's watching. That doesn't mean it's a business.

Future MBA case studies about this acquisition are going to need a trigger warning.

title: I just sat through a 2-hour 'innovation workshop' at my Fortune 500 company. The deliverable was a Post-It note that says 'leverage synergies.'
content:
I have just experienced something that I think constitutes a war crime under the Geneva Convention's lesser-known provisions about corporate time theft.

My company — a Fortune 500 that shall remain nameless but rhymes with 'we're terrified of startups' — has decided we need to be more innovative. Not actually innovative. We don't want to build anything new or take any risks or change any processes. We want to FEEL innovative. We want innovation theater.

So they brought in a consultant. This consultant charges $15,000 per day. PER DAY. I looked him up and his LinkedIn says he 'helps organizations unlock their innovation DNA.' That's not a real sentence. That's what happens when you put business buzzwords in a blender.

His first exercise was 'draw your feelings about the customer.' I am a backend engineer. I drew a stick figure crying. He said that was 'powerful.' I was drawing myself. He then asked us to 'empathize with the customer journey' by closing our eyes and imagining we were the customer. Thirty grown adults sat in a conference room with their eyes closed for four minutes. Someone fell asleep. The consultant called it 'deep empathy work.'

Then came the Post-It notes. Oh god, the Post-It notes. We were given 500 Post-It notes and told to write one idea per note. Any idea. No bad ideas. 'Blue sky thinking.' Someone wrote 'make the app faster.' Someone wrote 'better UX.' Someone wrote 'AI.' Just the word AI. Nothing else. The consultant put it on the wall and said 'yes, tell me more about this.' There was nothing more. It was two letters.

We then did 'dot voting' where we put stickers on our favorite ideas. The winning idea, with seven dots, was 'leverage synergies across business units.' That's not an idea. That's a sentence from a 2003 McKinsey deck. That's what you say when you have nothing to say but you need to fill a slide.

The consultant then had us do a 'rapid prototyping sprint' which consisted of drawing boxes on paper and calling them 'wireframes.' I drew a box with a smaller box inside it. The consultant said it showed 'strong design instinct.' It was a login page. Every login page in history looks like that.

The session ended with our VP of Strategy saying this was 'exactly the kind of thinking we need to take us to the next level.' WHAT LEVEL. We produced ONE Post-It note in two hours. The Post-It note says 'leverage synergies.' We spent $15,000 on a piece of paper that says the corporate equivalent of 'do business better.'

But here's the REAL kicker. This is part of a TWELVE SESSION engagement. They're coming back eleven more times. That's $180,000. For Post-It notes. We just had a round of layoffs where we let go of 200 people to 'optimize operational efficiency' and we're spending $180,000 on a man who tells engineers to draw their feelings.

I have never been more certain that large companies deserve to be disrupted. Not by startups. By anyone. By a particularly motivated raccoon. The bar is that low.
source_title: Corporate innovation workshops are a $12 billion industry built on Post-It notes

title: The entire crypto industry just pivoted to AI and nobody is acknowledging how funny that is
content:
I need everyone to stop what they're doing and appreciate what's happening right now because it is genuinely one of the funniest things I've witnessed in my 15 years in tech.

Remember crypto? Remember Web3? Remember when every single person at every single tech event was telling you that the future was decentralized and trustless and on the blockchain? Remember NFTs? Remember when someone paid $2.9 million for a picture of a rock? Remember DAOs? Remember when a DAO tried to buy the Constitution?

All those people. Every single one of them. They are now AI people.

It happened overnight. One day my feed was full of people saying 'few understand' about Ethereum layer 2 rollups. The next day the EXACT same people were saying 'few understand' about transformer architectures. They changed their Twitter bios from 'Web3 builder' to 'AI builder.' Some of them didn't even change their profile pictures. Same laser eyes. Now the laser eyes are for AI.

My buddy's 'Web3 decentralized social platform' is now an 'AI-powered content intelligence engine.' He changed the landing page and the pitch deck. The product is the same. It still doesn't work. But now it doesn't work with AI branding instead of blockchain branding, and apparently that's worth a higher valuation because investors have also pivoted from crypto to AI.

I went to a tech conference last month. At LEAST six booths had banners that still said 'blockchain' with a paper sign taped over it that said 'AI.' I am not exaggerating. One of them still had a QR code that went to their old whitepaper about tokenomics. They said they were 'updating the docs.'

The VCs are the funniest part. The same partners who were writing blog posts called 'Why Every Company Will Be a Web3 Company by 2025' are now writing posts called 'Why Every Company Will Be an AI Company by 2027.' They didn't even change the structure. Same post. Different buzzword. Find and replace. I checked — one VC literally has a post from 2022 about 'the Web3 stack every founder needs to know' and a post from 2024 about 'the AI stack every founder needs to know.' Same author. Same publication. Same confidence. Zero self-awareness.

The crypto conferences rebranded too. There's an event that was called 'DeFi Summit' two years ago. It's now called 'AI+DeFi Summit.' They kept DeFi in there as a vestigial organ. Like a tech appendix. It does nothing but they haven't removed it yet.

The absolute PEAK of this was a project I found that is — I promise I'm not making this up — an 'AI agent that trades crypto autonomously using blockchain-verified reasoning.' It's both. It's the turducken of hype cycles. They got AI AND crypto in there. They're double-dipping on the buzzword buffet.

Don't get me wrong. AI is real technology with real applications. But a LOT of the people who are now 'building in AI' are the same people who were 'building in Web3' and before that were 'building in the metaverse' and before that were 'building in VR.' They're not building anything. They're SURFING. They surf from hype wave to hype wave and the product never ships and the landing page always looks incredible and they're always 'in stealth' and they always have 50,000 Twitter followers.

I give it two years before whatever the next thing is and they all pivot again. My money is on quantum computing or biotech. Same people. Same laser eyes. Same 'few understand.'

title: I got rejected from a company, then they messaged me 6 months later saying they're 'excited to reconnect.' They are not excited. Nobody has ever been excited about a LinkedIn InMail.
content:
Let me walk you through the most absurd six months of my professional life because I think it perfectly captures what tech hiring has become.

January: I apply to a company. Let's call them TechCorp. I'm a senior full-stack dev with 9 years of experience. My resume is clean. My GitHub is active. I apply through their website.

February: No response. I follow up via email. Auto-reply says they're 'reviewing applications carefully to ensure the best fit for both parties.' Translation: nobody has looked at this.

March: I get an email from a recruiter. She's 'really excited about my background.' She wants to schedule an 'initial culture screen.' I take a 30-minute call where someone asks me what my favorite programming language is and why. I say TypeScript and give reasons. She says 'great energy.'

April: Technical phone screen. I solve two LeetCode mediums in 35 minutes. The interviewer says 'nice job' and I move forward.

April (still): Take-home assignment. They want me to build a 'small project' to demonstrate my skills. The spec is 4 pages long. It has database requirements, API requirements, frontend requirements, testing requirements, and a section on 'documentation and code quality.' It takes me 12 HOURS across a weekend. I submit it with a README, tests, CI config, and a deployed demo.

May: System design interview. I design a distributed notification system on a whiteboard for 90 minutes. Two behavioral rounds where I use the STAR method so many times I start to feel like a middle school guidance counselor. A coding round where I pair program with someone who types at 20 WPM. A 'culture fit' conversation with a director who looked like he'd rather be anywhere else on planet Earth. He asked me 'where do you see yourself in 5 years' and I almost said 'still interviewing for this position apparently.'

June: 'Meet the team' Zoom call. Six engineers on a video call for 45 minutes. Everyone is nice. I like the team. They seem to like me. Good vibes. I am cautiously optimistic.

June (two weeks later): Rejection email. Generic template. 'After careful consideration we've decided to move forward with candidates whose experience more closely aligns with our current needs.' I email the recruiter asking for specific feedback. She says they wanted 'more experience with their specific tech stack.'

Their tech stack is React and Node.

I HAVE NINE YEARS OF REACT AND NODE.

I spent 12 hours on a take-home, took a day off work for interviews, went through SIX rounds, and got rejected for not having enough experience in the TWO most common technologies in web development. I've been writing React since class components. I've been writing Node since before async/await. I was using Express when their company didn't EXIST.

December: LinkedIn InMail. Same company. Different recruiter. 'Hi [my name], I came across your profile and I'm really excited to reconnect about a senior full-stack role at TechCorp!'

EXCITED. TO. RECONNECT.

You're not excited. You had layoffs. Three of the people on that 'meet the team' Zoom are gone. I checked LinkedIn. You're backfilling. You burned through your top candidates with your 6-round interview gauntlet and now you're going back to the reject pile and pretending you're doing ME a favor.

I didn't respond. I thought about responding with just a screenshot of the rejection email. I thought about responding with an invoice for the 12-hour take-home at my consulting rate. I thought about a lot of things.

Instead I just stared at the message for ten minutes, closed LinkedIn, and mass-applied to 40 jobs. Three of them responded. None of them were excited. Nobody is excited. The entire tech hiring process is a theater of manufactured enthusiasm followed by automated rejection followed by amnesia.

If you're going through this right now, just know it's not you. The system is broken. Your skills are fine. The process is insane. And nobody — NOBODY — has ever been genuinely excited about a LinkedIn InMail.
source_title: Analysis: Corporate Recruiting Tools Mask Disengagement With Automated 'Excitement'

title: Microsoft just put ads in the Windows Start Menu. We are living in the dystopia but it's boring instead of cool.
content:
Remember when an operating system just... operated? Like, that was the whole job. You turned on your computer and it said 'hey, here's your desktop, go do your thing.' That was it. That was the social contract.

I booted up my laptop this morning and before I could open a browser, Windows suggested I try Bing, reminded me about OneDrive, recommended Candy Crush, and asked if I wanted to set up Microsoft Copilot. I just want to open Excel, man. I JUST WANT TO OPEN EXCEL.

I've been a Windows user since 3.1. I watched this happen in slow motion like a car crash that takes 30 years. Windows XP was peak. Clean start menu. No opinions. It just sat there and let you work. Then Vista happened and we should have seen the writing on the wall, but we forgave them because 7 was good. We got COMPLACENT.

Now I click the Start Menu and it's like walking into a bazaar. There are suggestions. There are recommendations. There are 'tips' that are just ads wearing a fake mustache. I uninstalled three apps I never installed yesterday. THREE. Where did they come from? Who put them there? I didn't consent to having Spotify pinned to my taskbar. I don't even USE Spotify on this machine.

And the Settings app. Oh god, the Settings app. Half the settings are still in the old Control Panel, which they've been 'deprecating' for A DECADE, and the new Settings app has a 'recommended' section that is literally just Microsoft products. 'Hey, have you tried Microsoft 365? Have you tried Microsoft Teams? Have you tried giving us more money for the thing you already paid for?'

I paid $139 for Windows 11 Pro. PRO. The professional version. And it has ads. I paid full price for software that serves me advertisements. We used to call that malware. Literally. If a program installed itself without your consent and showed you ads, you ran Malwarebytes on it. Now it IS the operating system.

My favorite part is the copilot button they added to the keyboard on new laptops. A PHYSICAL HARDWARE BUTTON for their AI assistant that nobody asked for. You can't even remap it easily. It's just there. Watching. Waiting. I hit it by accident three times a day and it opens this sidebar that wants to 'help me be more productive' while being the single biggest source of lost productivity in my workflow.

The real kicker? I looked into switching to Linux last weekend. Spent four hours configuring stuff, got my printer working on the third attempt, then realized I need Adobe products for work and crawled back to Windows like a dog returning to its owner after being scolded. Microsoft KNOWS this. They know we can't leave. That's why the ads keep coming. We're trapped in a abusive relationship with an operating system and the operating system just put a billboard in our living room.

We were promised a cyberpunk dystopia with neon lights and cool hacking. Instead we got Candy Crush ads in the Start Menu. The dystopia is here and it's just... boring. It's SO boring. The machines didn't rise up against us. They just started showing us targeted advertising and we accepted it because the alternative is learning how to partition a drive in Arch Linux.

title: Every tech company is a 'platform' now. My local sandwich shop has a developer API. I wish I was joking.
content:
The sandwich shop near my office launched a developer API last month. I am not making this up. It's called the SubStack (yes, really) and it lets you programmatically order sandwiches. It has documentation. It has rate limiting. It has OAuth 2.0. The turkey club requires authentication. I need to pass a Bearer token to get extra pickles.

There's a Swagger page. For sandwiches. I can GET /menu/sandwiches and it returns a JSON array of sandwich objects with nested ingredient arrays. The meatball sub has a schema. There's an enum for bread types. Someone sat down and decided that 'WHEAT', 'WHITE', 'RYE', 'SOURDOUGH', and 'WRAP' needed to be programmatically enumerated.

They have a developer community Discord. FOURTEEN PEOPLE ARE IN IT. One of them built a Slack integration so his team can order lunch without leaving their standup. Another one made a CLI tool called 'sammich' that you install via npm. It has 3 GitHub stars. All three are from people who work at the sandwich shop.

But here's the thing - this isn't even the most unhinged example anymore. EVERYTHING is a platform now. My dentist's office has a 'developer portal.' My dry cleaner sends me webhooks. WEBHOOKS. When my shirts are ready, I get a POST request to a URL I never configured. My laundry has an event-driven architecture.

I talked to the sandwich shop owner about it and he said, and I quote, 'We're not really a sandwich company anymore, we're a food logistics platform that happens to make sandwiches.' SIR. You have FOUR EMPLOYEES. One of them is your nephew. You are a SANDWICH SHOP. You make SANDWICHES. The sandwiches are GOOD. You don't need a platform. YOU NEED BREAD AND MEAT AND A KNIFE.

He told me they're working on a marketplace where other sandwich shops can list their menus through his API. He called it 'Sandwich-as-a-Service.' He has a pitch deck. I've seen the pitch deck. There's a slide about TAM (Total Addressable Mouths). I wish I were joking about any of this but I'm not and I can't even be mad because the Italian combo is genuinely excellent.

The worst part? His API is actually well-designed. Better than some enterprise APIs I've worked with professionally. The error messages are clear. The pagination works correctly. He has proper versioning. Meanwhile at my actual job, our internal API returns 200 OK with an error message in the body and nobody thinks this is a problem.

We have reached peak platform brain. A coffee shop in my neighborhood describes itself as 'a beverage ecosystem.' A DOG GROOMER I follow on Instagram just announced their 'partner program.' I got an email from my mechanic about their 'API roadmap for Q3.' The mechanic. The guy who changes my oil wants me to know about his API roadmap.

I give it six months before someone launches a developer conference for sandwich APIs. It'll be called BreadConf or SubSummit and it'll sell out because of course it will. We deserve this. We did this to ourselves. Every programmer who ever said 'everything should have an API' manifested this cursed reality and now we have to live in it.

Anyway the sandwich shop's rate limit is 10 requests per minute which honestly seems reasonable for sandwich ordering. I've never needed to order more than 10 sandwiches in a minute. If you do, there's an enterprise tier. It's $49/month. It comes with priority toasting.
source_title: The API Economy Reaches Main Street as Local Shops Rush to Build Developer Platforms

title: I just paid $1,200 for a phone that's 0.3mm thinner than last year's model. I have been successfully marketed to and I accept my fate.
content:
Let me walk you through the exact sequence of events that led to me giving a trillion-dollar corporation $1,200 for a rectangle that is imperceptibly thinner than the rectangle I already owned.

Step 1: I watched the keynote. I KNOW I shouldn't watch the keynotes. Every year I say I won't watch the keynote. Every year I watch the keynote. They spent 20 minutes talking about the new camera system. I take pictures of my dog and my food. The dog doesn't care about computational photography and the pasta doesn't need ProRAW. But they showed a photo of a sunset and I thought 'wow, my sunsets could look like that.' MY SUNSETS ALREADY LOOK LIKE THAT. The human eye cannot distinguish the difference. I compared photos from my old phone and the new one side by side and my wife said 'those look the same' and she's RIGHT.

Step 2: They said the word 'titanium' about forty-seven times. My brain, which is apparently made of soup, heard 'titanium' and thought 'oh that's the strong metal from the aerospace industry, I need that for my device that I will use primarily to look at Twitter on the toilet.' I have never once been in a situation where I thought 'I wish my phone were made of a stronger aerospace alloy.' I've dropped it onto carpet. That's the most extreme environment it's been in. Carpet.

Step 3: The chip. The new chip is '40% faster' at something. I don't know what. I don't do anything on my phone that requires 40% more speed. I scroll. I text. I take the aforementioned dog and pasta photos. My PREVIOUS chip was already so fast that the bottleneck in my phone experience was my THUMB. But they showed a graph where a bar was bigger than another bar and my lizard brain said 'big bar good.'

Step 4: They announced the price and I felt a brief moment of clarity. $1,200. For a phone. That's rent in some cities. That's a plane ticket to Europe. That's 400 sandwiches from the shop down the street (they have an API now but that's another post). For one shining moment I thought 'this is absurd, I don't need this, my current phone works perfectly.' That moment lasted about 11 seconds.

Step 5: I pre-ordered it at 5 AM. I set an ALARM to pre-order a phone. I woke up before dawn to give Apple money. My wife asked why my alarm was going off and I said 'don't worry about it' like I was committing a crime, and honestly the financial impact was similar.

The phone arrived. I transferred everything over. It looks identical. It feels identical, except 0.3mm thinner, which I absolutely cannot perceive with my human hands. The camera takes photos that look exactly the same as my old photos. The screen is the same. The battery lasts roughly the same amount of time. I spent $1,200 for what is effectively a software update with a new case.

AND I ALREADY KNOW I'LL DO IT AGAIN NEXT YEAR. That's the worst part. I'm not even mad at Apple. I'm mad at myself. I'm mad at the part of my brain that sees a slightly different shade of 'Space Black' and thinks 'yes, THIS is the one that will finally complete me as a person.' I'm a 34-year-old adult with a mortgage and I'm out here acting like a new phone will change my life. It will not change my life. Nothing has changed. My dog still looks the same in photos. The pasta still looks the same. I'm just $1,200 poorer and 0.3mm thinner.

The only genuine upgrade is the USB-C port and I could have gotten that by buying last year's model. I am a cautionary tale and I am telling you this from my new phone which is, I must admit, very nice to hold.

title: LinkedIn has become Facebook for people who wear lanyards. I saw a post today that said 'I fired my best employee and here's why that made me a better leader.' Sir this is a professional network.
content:
I need to talk about what is happening on LinkedIn because I feel like I'm losing my mind and I need to know if other people are seeing this too.

Yesterday I saw a CEO post a picture of himself crying at his desk with the caption 'Sometimes leaders need to feel.' It had 47,000 likes. FORTY-SEVEN THOUSAND. The comments were all 'So brave' and 'This is what real leadership looks like.' He was crying because his Series B got delayed by two weeks. TWO WEEKS. The man owns a boat. He posted a picture of the boat three days earlier. He is fine. But there he was, tears streaming down his face, photographed from a SUSPICIOUSLY good angle for someone who is supposedly in the throes of genuine emotion. Someone either took that photo for him or he set up a tripod. Either way, sir, this is a professional network.

The post archetypes on LinkedIn have become so predictable I could write a bot to generate them. Actually someone probably has. Here they are:

1. THE HUMBLEFIRE: 'I just got laid off and it's the best thing that ever happened to me.' Posted 4 hours after getting fired. Already has a new headshot. Brother you have not even updated your resume yet, maybe process the grief before you start content marketing your own termination.

2. THE PARABLE: 'I was in line at Starbucks and the barista said something that changed my entire approach to leadership.' No she didn't. She said 'grande or venti' and you said 'grande' and then you sat down and made up a fake inspirational story for engagement.

3. THE COUNTER-INTUITIVE TAKE: 'I fired my best employee and here's why that made me a better leader.' These are always absolutely UNHINGED. The story never adds up. The 'lesson' is always something like 'sometimes you have to let go of excellence to make room for growth' which means absolutely nothing. You fired someone who was good at their job and now you want a round of applause? FROM THE PROFESSIONAL NETWORK?

4. THE AGREE?: Every post ends with 'Agree?' or 'Thoughts?' Like they're fishing for engagement by making you feel obligated to respond. 'I think companies should treat employees like humans. Agree?' YES. OBVIOUSLY. You have not said anything controversial. You've just stated a basic premise of civilization and acted like it's a hot take.

5. THE BROETRY: Short sentences. Each one its own line. For dramatic. Effect. Like this. Every post. Reads like. A spoken word. Poem. About synergy. And it always ends with something like 'That's the power of believing in yourself' as if reformatting your text into a poetic structure makes 'work hard and be nice' a groundbreaking insight.

I saw a guy post 'I gave my employees UNLIMITED PTO and here's what happened' and the answer was 'they took less PTO than before because of the implicit social pressure of an undefined system' and he framed this as a WIN. My man just described a system that made his employees take FEWER vacations and he's out here acting like he solved work-life balance.

The influencer accounts are the worst. There are people whose entire job is LinkedIn content. They post three times a day about 'leadership' and 'culture' and 'disruption' and they've never built anything. Their entire career IS the LinkedIn posts. It's content about content. It's a snake eating its own lanyard.

My favorite recent genre is the 'I asked ChatGPT to write my resume and the results were SHOCKING' posts. They're all clearly written by ChatGPT. The AI is writing posts about itself on a platform full of people pretending to have emotions about quarterly revenue targets. We've achieved some kind of singularity but it's not the cool kind, it's the LinkedIn kind, where everything is fake and the points don't matter but everyone acts like they do.

I keep saying I'm going to delete my account but I can't because apparently employers still think it's important and my recruiter said I need to 'maintain a presence.' So here I am. Maintaining a presence. Watching a man cry about his Series B. On a Tuesday.

title: We spent $2.3 million migrating to microservices. We now have 47 services, 200 Kubernetes pods, and the same bugs we had before, just distributed across more containers.
content:
I need to tell this story because I've been holding it in for two years and my therapist says I should 'express my frustrations in a constructive way' and she doesn't know what Kubernetes is so this is the next best thing.

In 2024, our CTO read a blog post. That's it. That's the inciting incident of a $2.3 million migration that consumed our engineering team for 18 months. The blog post was titled something like 'Why We Moved to Microservices and You Should Too' and it was written by an engineer at a company with 4,000 employees and 50 million daily active users. We have 40 employees and our peak traffic is like 200 concurrent users during a product launch. But the CTO read this blog post and came into the Monday standup and said the words that still haunt me: 'I think we need to break up the monolith.'

THE MONOLITH WAS FINE. I want to be very clear about this. Our monolith was a perfectly functional Rails app. It had problems, sure. Every codebase has problems. But the problems were KNOWABLE. When something broke, I checked one log file. ONE. I opened one terminal, I tailed one log, and I could see what happened. The entire debugging cycle was: something breaks, check log, find error, fix error, deploy. Total time: maybe 30 minutes.

Now? Now when something breaks, I check 47 log files, three monitoring dashboards, two distributed tracing systems, and a Slack channel where someone inevitably says 'works on my cluster.' Our deployment pipeline takes 4 hours. It USED to take 8 minutes. Eight. Minutes. I used to deploy and go get a coffee. Now I deploy and go get a DEGREE.

Here's what we have now: 47 microservices. Each one has its own repo, its own CI pipeline, its own deployment config, its own Helm chart, its own set of environment variables that are SLIGHTLY different from every other service. We have a service for users, a service for auth, a service for notifications, a service for emails, a service for 'email templates' (separate from emails, don't ask), a service for analytics, a service for billing, a service for 'billing events' (SEPARATE FROM BILLING), and I swear to god we have a service whose only job is to tell other services what time it is.

The network calls. Oh god, the network calls. What used to be a function call within a single process is now an HTTP request across a network. Do you know what networks do? They FAIL. They have LATENCY. A page load that used to hit one database query now hits 14 services in sequence because some architect decided that the user profile page needs to independently fetch the user from the user service, the avatar from the media service, the preferences from the preferences service, and the display name from - I am not making this up - the 'identity resolution service.' IT'S A DISPLAY NAME. IT'S IN THE USERS TABLE. OR IT WAS, BEFORE WE SPLIT THE USERS TABLE ACROSS FOUR SERVICES.

We had to hire a full-time platform team. Three engineers whose entire job is keeping Kubernetes running. Before microservices, we didn't have a platform team. We had a guy named Dave who ran the deploys and also did backend work. Dave was enough. Dave was MORE than enough. Now Dave leads a team of three people and they spend all day writing YAML. So much YAML. I have seen things in YAML that would make a grown developer weep. Our Kubernetes configs are longer than the actual application code.

The costs. Our AWS bill went from $8,000/month to $47,000/month. Each service needs its own load balancer, its own cluster resources, its own monitoring. We're paying for 200 pods to serve 200 users. THAT'S ONE POD PER USER. I could literally hire a person to manually handle each user's requests and it might be cheaper.

And the BUGS. The beautiful, beautiful bugs. We have all the same bugs we had before. Every single one. The payment processing race condition? Still there, just now it happens across a network boundary so it's HARDER to reproduce. The notification duplication issue? Still there, but now it involves a message queue so instead of sending two emails it sometimes sends two hundred. We didn't fix a single bug during the migration. We just gave them all new addresses.

The best part is the meetings. We now have a weekly 'service owners sync' where 47 service owners meet to discuss cross-service dependencies. It's 90 minutes long. It used to be unnecessary because all the code was in one place and you could just READ IT. Now if I want to understand how a feature works end-to-end, I have to trace it through seven repos, four message queues, two API gateways, and a 'service mesh' that I don't fully understand and at this point I'm afraid to ask.

Two weeks ago our CEO asked why a simple feature request was estimated at 6 weeks. I had to explain that changing a dropdown menu now requires coordinating deploys across three services, updating two API contracts, modifying a shared protobuf definition, and getting approval from two service owners who are on different sprint cycles. He stared at me for a long time. I stared back. We both knew what had happened. Neither of us said it.

The monolith was fine. The monolith was FINE. If you're reading this and your CTO just discovered a blog post about microservices, run. Take the monolith and RUN.
source_title: The $2.3 Million Migration: How One Company's Microservices Journey Reveals Industry-Wide Delusion

title: The VC who told me my startup was 'too niche' just invested $30M in an app that rates public bathrooms. I'm done.
content:
I need to vent because I am losing my MIND.

Last year I pitched a B2B supply chain optimization tool to about 40 VCs. We had $800k ARR, 40% margins, enterprise clients who were literally begging us to take their money, and a 94% retention rate. Every single meeting ended the same way: 'Love the team, love the traction, but the market is just too niche for us.'

Too. Niche.

Fast forward to last week. I see on TechCrunch that one of those EXACT same VCs just led a $30M Series A for an app called — and I wish I was making this up — BathroomDAO. It is an app that lets you rate public bathrooms. On the blockchain. Their pitch deck, which someone leaked on Twitter, had a slide called 'The Flush Economy.' I am not being metaphorical. That was the ACTUAL slide title. There was a tokenomics diagram shaped like a toilet.

But wait, it gets better. I did some digging. In the same quarter that my profitable, growing B2B SaaS was 'too niche,' the following companies raised money from funds that passed on me:

- An AI-powered app that tells you what your dog is thinking ($12M seed)
- A startup that delivers single ice cubes on demand for craft cocktails ($8M Series A, they call it 'IceAAS' — Ice as a Service)
- A social network exclusively for people named Josh ($4.5M pre-seed, and yes this is the ACTUAL product)

Meanwhile my supply chain tool is saving manufacturers an average of $2.3M per year and I'm funding it with credit cards and prayers.

I finally got an honest answer from a VC friend after three beers. He said, and I quote: 'Your problem is that your company makes sense. We can't put a sensible company in our deck. LPs want to see bets on the future, and the future has to sound insane or it's not ambitious enough.'

So the investment thesis is literally: if it sounds reasonable, it's not venture-scale, but if it sounds like something a crazy person would pitch on Shark Tank at 3 AM, here's thirty million dollars.

I'm going back to my garage to build something that absolutely no one needs. Thinking about an app that uses satellite imagery to rank people's lawns. Gonna call it GrassDAO. Expect my seed round announcement next quarter.

EDIT: Three VCs have already DMed me asking if GrassDAO is real. I hate it here.

title: Your 'smart' home is just 47 devices that stop working when the WiFi goes out and I am BEGGING you to see the irony
content:
Our internet went out for six hours last night and I got to experience what it's like to live in a $400,000 house that is DUMBER than a cave.

My wife asked me to turn on the kitchen lights. Simple request, right? WRONG. The lights are Hue bulbs. They require the Hue Bridge. The Hue Bridge requires WiFi. The WiFi requires the router. The router had crashed and needed a firmware update. The firmware update required me to connect to the router's local admin page. Which required the lights to be on so I could see the tiny reset button on the back of the router that's wedged behind the bookshelf.

So to turn on the lights I needed the lights to already be on. We ate dinner by candlelight like it was 1847. The smart candle was also offline.

But it gets SO much worse. Here is a comprehensive list of things that stopped functioning in my home when the WiFi went out:

- All lights (67 smart bulbs, zero dumb switches left because I REMOVED THEM LIKE AN IDIOT)
- Thermostat (it was 42 degrees outside, the Nest showed a sad face and gave up)
- Front door lock (my mother-in-law was outside for 20 minutes, which honestly was the one bright spot)
- Garage door (my car was IMPRISONED)
- The stove (why does a STOVE need WiFi? WHY DID I BUY A STOVE WITH WIFI?)
- Both toilets (they have bidets with app-controlled settings, I will not elaborate further)
- The robot vacuum, which was mid-cycle and just stopped in the hallway like it died
- The baby monitor (had to physically walk to the baby's room and USE MY EYES like a PEASANT)

My 74-year-old neighbor saw me standing in my driveway trying to get cell signal to operate my own garage door and said 'You know, my house has switches.' He said it with such pity. Such gentle, devastating pity.

I have spent roughly $14,000 making my home 'smart' and all it took was a Comcast outage to reduce me to a man standing in his own kitchen holding a match, unable to flush his toilet, locked out of his garage, wearing three sweaters because the thermostat thinks it's not connected to a house anymore.

I'm going to Home Depot tomorrow and buying the dumbest light switches they sell. The ones that go up and down. With my HAND. Like an ANIMAL. And I will be FREE.

The irony is that 'smart home' technology has made us entirely dependent on the dumbest, least reliable piece of infrastructure we own: the ISP. Congratulations, we automated our houses and gave the kill switch to Comcast.

EDIT: The WiFi came back on and every single device needed to be re-paired. I have been at this for four hours. The robot vacuum drove itself into the pool.
source_title: Smart Home Reliability Gap Threatens $174 Billion Market as Outages Expose Flaws

title: TikTok's algorithm figured out I'm having a midlife crisis before my therapist did. Is this a privacy violation or a public service?
content:
I need to talk about something that happened to me last Tuesday because it has fundamentally shaken my understanding of privacy, technology, and my own psyche.

I opened TikTok — something I do purely for 'research purposes' as a 39-year-old man — and the first five videos on my For You page were, in this EXACT order:

1. A guy restoring a vintage 1972 Honda CB350 motorcycle in his garage, no talking, just vibes
2. A therapist explaining 'how to talk to your kids when you and your spouse are growing apart'
3. A financial advisor doing a video called 'Starting Over at 40: It's Not Too Late to Build Wealth'
4. A real estate listing for a cabin in Montana with 40 acres, no neighbors, and a wood-burning stove
5. A sourdough starter tutorial

I have told TikTok NOTHING. I have never searched for any of these topics. I have never liked a video about motorcycles, therapy, divorce, Montana, or bread. I don't even eat bread. I'm doing low carb. Or I WAS doing low carb until TikTok showed me that sourdough video and I watched it seven times.

But here's what's terrifying: it was ALL accurate. Every single video was something I needed to see. I HAVE been thinking about getting a motorcycle. My wife and I HAVE been distant lately. I HAVE been anxious about retirement savings. I HAVE fantasized about disappearing to a cabin in the woods. And apparently I DO want to make sourdough, which I did not know until an algorithm told me.

My therapist, who I've been seeing for THREE YEARS and who I PAY $200 AN HOUR, still thinks my main issue is 'work stress.' TikTok diagnosed my entire existential crisis in 45 seconds of scrolling. For free.

So I started paying attention. Over the next week, TikTok served me:
- Videos about men who quit corporate jobs to become woodworkers (watched all of them)
- A guy explaining how your metabolism changes at 40 (ATTACKED)
- Content about 'gray divorce' trends (I googled this at 2 AM and I am not okay)
- Three different videos about buying land in rural Vermont
- An ad for hair loss treatment (UNCALLED FOR but... accurate)

I haven't clicked, liked, or searched for ANY of these things. The algorithm is reading my face. Or my scrolling speed. Or the micro-hesitations in my thumb. Or it's pulling data from some dimension I don't understand. Maybe my phone heard me sigh.

The real question I'm wrestling with: Is this a horrifying privacy invasion, or did a Chinese social media app just save me $15,000 in therapy by showing me who I actually am in under a minute? Because my therapist was going to get to the midlife crisis thing eventually, probably around 2028, and TikTok just speedran my entire psychological profile between a cat video and someone pressure-washing a driveway.

I'm now 6 videos deep into a Montana real estate TikTok account and I have a sourdough starter named Gerald fermenting on my kitchen counter. The algorithm has won. I am its puppet. Gerald is rising nicely though.

EDIT: My wife found this post. She said 'the algorithm is right.' I'm going to go feed Gerald.

title: GitHub Copilot just autocompleted my resignation letter while I was writing a function. Even the AI knows.
content:
So I'm at my desk at 11:47 PM on a Wednesday, working on a sprint that was supposed to end last Friday but got 'extended' because the PM added 14 tickets at 4:59 PM on Thursday, and I start writing a function.

The function is called shouldContinue(). It's for a retry loop in our payment processing service. Standard stuff. I type the function signature, and GitHub Copilot — my AI pair programmer, my digital colleague, the only entity at this company that works as many hours as I do — suggests the following implementation:

    return false;

That's it. That was the entire suggestion. `return false.`

I stared at it for a solid 30 seconds. The cursor blinked. The office was empty. Somewhere a Slack notification chimed for a message I already knew said 'quick question' followed by something that was neither quick nor a question.

The AI wasn't wrong.

But it gets better. I dismissed the suggestion and started writing the actual logic. I typed a comment: `// check if we should` and Copilot autocompleted it to `// check if we should even be doing this anymore`. I am not making this up. I have the screenshot. The AI is having an existential crisis on my behalf.

Later that night I was writing error handling and typed `throw new` and it suggested `throw new Error('I cannot do this anymore')`. At this point I'm genuinely unsure if Copilot is reading my codebase or my SOUL.

This sent me down a rabbit hole of asking other devs about their Copilot moments and apparently this is A THING:

- A friend typed `// TODO:` and Copilot completed it with `// TODO: find a job that respects work-life balance`
- Someone on Twitter said they wrote `getUserHappiness()` and got `return null;`
- A coworker typed `const deadline =` and Copilot suggested `new Date('never')`

Look, I know it's just pattern matching on billions of lines of code written by millions of burnt-out developers. That's what makes it so devastating. Copilot isn't sentient. It's just trained on the collective despair of every software engineer who ever pushed code at midnight on a Sunday because someone said the word 'urgent' in a Slack channel. It's not AI consciousness. It's AI DEPRESSION, aggregated from our entire profession's source code.

We literally wrote so much sad, burnt-out code that the AI learned hopelessness as a programming pattern.

I've been a developer for 12 years. In that time I've watched this industry go from 'we're changing the world' to '14 standups a week and your OKRs are misaligned.' I've adopted every methodology that promised to make things better — Agile, then Scrum, then SAFe, then whatever fresh hell comes next — and every single one just added more meetings and more Jira tickets.

My calendar tomorrow has 6 hours of meetings, a 'mandatory fun' team-building exercise where we're going to do an escape room (the irony is DEAFENING), and a 1:1 with my manager where he'll ask me why the sprint velocity is down while I silently calculate how many artisan candles I'd need to sell on Etsy to match my salary.

Anyway I accepted the `return false` suggestion. The tests pass. The function works. Copilot and I have an understanding now.

EDIT: Just typed `const yearsUntilRetirement =` and Copilot suggested `Infinity`. I'm going to bed.

title: Netflix raised prices again and removed the show I was watching mid-season. They want me to pirate. They are BEGGING me to pirate.
content:
Let me walk you through my evening last night so you can understand the FULL scope of what the streaming industry has done to us.

7:00 PM — I sit down to watch the next episode of a show I've been watching on Netflix. It's gone. Not cancelled. Not moved to a different tab. GONE. Removed from the platform entirely. Mid-season. Episode 6 of 10. I will never know what happened to those characters. They exist in a narrative purgatory now, frozen forever in the cliffhanger of episode 5. I paid for this.

7:05 PM — I google where the show went. It's now on Peacock. PEACOCK. A streaming service I refuse to acknowledge exists on principle.

7:10 PM — Fine. I'll watch something else. I search for a movie my friend recommended. It's on HBO Max. Wait, it's just called 'Max' now. No wait, is it HBO again? I don't know what it's called this week. I don't have it regardless.

7:15 PM — I open Disney+ to watch a Star Wars show. Disney+ now has ads on my tier. I am paying $13.99 a month to watch advertisements. My grandfather would be HORRIFIED and he watched actual broadcast television that was FREE.

7:20 PM — I try Hulu. Hulu is now inside Disney+? Or is it still separate? Somehow I'm paying for both and neither works properly.

7:30 PM — I decide to just watch The Office. It's not on Netflix (where it used to be). It's on Peacock (where I refuse to go). Wait, is it back on Netflix? Let me check. No. Maybe? Some seasons? I give up.

7:45 PM — I pull out a spreadsheet. I wish I was joking. Here is what I currently pay per month for streaming:

- Netflix (Standard): $17.99
- Disney+ (No Ads): $13.99
- HBO Max/Max/Whatever: $15.99
- Amazon Prime Video: $14.99
- Hulu (somehow separate from Disney+??): $17.99
- Apple TV+: $9.99
- Paramount+ (I forgot I had this): $11.99
- YouTube Premium (technically streaming): $13.99

TOTAL: $116.92/month. ONE HUNDRED AND SIXTEEN DOLLARS. PER MONTH.

My parents' cable bill in 2005 was $89/month and it had EVERYTHING. Every channel. Every show. One remote. One interface. One bill. You turned on the TV and stuff was ON.

I now pay 30% MORE than cable to have 8 different apps with 8 different interfaces, 8 different search functions that don't work, 8 different 'Continue Watching' lists, and 8 different recommendation algorithms that all think I want to watch true crime documentaries. I have to remember which app has which show, and the answer changes MONTHLY because they keep shuffling content around like a shell game designed to make me subscribe to Peacock.

And they keep RAISING PRICES while REMOVING CONTENT. Netflix just increased my plan by $2 for the privilege of having fewer shows than last year. That's like your landlord raising rent and removing a bathroom. 'We've increased your monthly payment and also the kitchen is gone now. It's on Peacock.'

The original pitch of streaming was: all the content, one place, cheap, no ads, watch whenever you want. What we have now is: fragmented content, eight places, expensive, ads are back, and the show you're watching might just VANISH because the licensing agreement expired on a Tuesday.

We have literally reinvented cable but worse. At least cable had channel surfing. I now spend 45 minutes scrolling through eight apps trying to find something to watch, and then I go to bed angry.

You know what has everything? You know what has every show, every movie, every season, no ads, one interface, and costs nothing? I think you know. We ALL know. And at this point the streaming companies aren't just failing to compete with it — they're actively running a marketing campaign for it.

I'm not saying I'm going to pirate. I'm saying that Netflix removed a show I was paying to watch mid-season and then raised my price by $2 in the same month, and if that isn't a formal written invitation to pirate, I don't know what is.

EDIT: Someone in the comments said 'just get a VPN and one service.' My brother in Christ, the shows I want are spread across FIVE services. The content is BALKANIZED. There is no one service to rule them all anymore. That was the whole point of this post.

EDIT 2: Netflix if you're reading this I would like my show back. I need to know if Detective Chen survived the warehouse explosion. PLEASE.
source_title: Netflix's latest moves are pushing subscribers straight to piracy sites

title: The metaverse cost $46 billion and the best they could show us was a legless avatar in an empty conference room. Incredible.
content:
Let me walk you through the timeline of the greatest money bonfire in tech history.

2021: Zuckerberg goes on stage and says the metaverse will be how we work, play, and socialize in the future. He literally renamed the entire company. Facebook, one of the most recognized brands on EARTH, became Meta. The stock dipped and he said trust the vision.

2022: They reveal Horizon Worlds. The avatars didn't have LEGS. They spent more than the GDP of Iceland and forgot LEGS. The demo looked like a Wii Sports lobby from 2006 except somehow worse because the Wii actually had good art direction. Someone pointed out that VRChat, made by like 12 people, had full-body avatars years ago. The internet roasted them so hard they had to rush out a legs update.

2023: Reality Labs is burning $4 billion PER QUARTER. That's $46 million a DAY. Every single day, the equivalent of a mid-size startup's entire funding round just evaporates into virtual conference rooms that nobody asked for and nobody uses.

The highlight reel of what $46 billion bought us: legless avatars attending meetings that could have been emails, a virtual Wendy's that somehow had worse service than real Wendy's, and Mark Zuckerberg's legs reveal which was treated as a PRODUCT ANNOUNCEMENT. A man showed the world that his cartoon avatar could now have legs and the press covered it like it was the moon landing.

Meanwhile the actual VR games people enjoy? Beat Saber. Made by a small Czech studio. Cost probably 0.001% of the metaverse budget. Has more daily active users than Horizon Worlds ever did.

The best part is the internal reports that leaked showing employees didn't even want to use their own product. The people BUILDING the metaverse wouldn't voluntarily ENTER the metaverse. If the chefs won't eat at their own restaurant, maybe the restaurant is bad.

But sure, let's keep going. Vision Pro exists now and costs $3,500 so you can watch movies alone while looking like a ski goggle model. The future is here and it's lonely and expensive.

I'm not saying VR will never be a thing. I'm saying maybe don't bet $46 billion on it before you figure out the legs situation.
source_title: Meta's $46 Billion Metaverse Gamble Yields Avatars Without Legs

title: I'm a senior dev making $300k and I still straight up Google 'how to center a div' at least once a week. We are all frauds. Every one of us.
content:
I need to get something off my chest and I think this is a safe space.

My LinkedIn says 'Full Stack Engineer' and 'distributed systems expert.' I have 11 years of experience. I've led teams. I've architected systems that handle millions of requests. I've given TALKS at conferences about microservice patterns.

Last Tuesday I spent 45 minutes debugging something that turned out to be a missing semicolon. The Tuesday before that I had to Google how to exit Vim. I've been using Vim for 8 years. I have a poster of Vim keybindings ON MY WALL. I looked at the poster, looked at my screen, and still opened a new terminal and killed the process.

Here's what nobody tells junior devs: the Googling never stops. It just gets more embarrassing. At year one you Google 'what is a for loop' and nobody judges you. At year eleven you Google 'javascript array sort not working' and find a Stack Overflow answer you UPVOTED in 2018 and still don't remember the solution.

I Google 'how to center a div' at least once a week. I have a BOOKMARK for it. Sometimes I open the bookmark, read the entire article, implement the solution, and then the next week I open the same bookmark again like it's brand new information. My brain simply refuses to store CSS knowledge. It's like RAM that gets cleared every 72 hours.

Last month a junior dev asked me to pair program. I sweated through the entire session because I knew—I KNEW—they were going to watch me type and see that I Google basic syntax. They did. They saw me Google 'python string reverse.' They were too polite to say anything. I could see the respect leaving their eyes in real time.

The impostor syndrome never goes away. It just evolves. First you think 'I don't belong here.' Then you get promoted and think 'I DEFINITELY don't belong here.' Then you get promoted again and think 'this is getting ridiculous, someone is going to find out.' Then you become the person interviewing candidates and you realize OH NO, everyone else is also just barely holding it together.

I interviewed a candidate last week who apologized for not knowing an obscure React hook from memory. Brother, I designed a system that processes 2 million events per day and last Friday I had to ask ChatGPT what the difference between map and forEach was. You're doing fine.

We are all frauds. Every single one of us. The only difference between a junior dev and a senior dev is that the senior dev Googles things faster and has learned to nod confidently while doing it.
source_title: Senior developers rely on search engines for basic tasks, study finds

title: Every startup's 'About Us' page is the same stock photo of diverse people high-fiving around a MacBook and I need it to stop
content:
I have a challenge for you. Go visit 10 random startup websites right now. I'll wait.

Done? Great. Let me guess what you saw.

Every single one had: a hero section with a gradient from purple to blue (or occasionally purple to pink for the BOLD ones), the word 'reimagine' in the headline, a photo of people who clearly do not work there looking absolutely DELIGHTED at a laptop screen, three feature cards with abstract geometric icons that convey no information, a 'Trusted by' section with logos that were definitely not permission-granted, and a CTA button that says 'Get Started' in a rounded rectangle.

I work in design and I am losing my mind. I visited a startup that sells B2B inventory management software and their hero image was a woman laughing while holding a salad. MA'AM. You sell WAREHOUSE SOFTWARE. Why is there a SALAD.

The About Us pages are where it gets truly unhinged. They all have the same stock photo of six impossibly attractive people of perfectly calculated demographic diversity gathered around a single MacBook, pointing at the screen and high-fiving like they just cured a disease. In reality, if six people gathered around one laptop at any actual company, four of them would be checking their phones and one would be asking if this could have been a Slack message.

And the COPY. Oh god, the copy. 'We're on a mission to reimagine how the world thinks about [extremely boring thing].' No you're not. You made a SaaS tool for expense tracking. That's fine. That's a perfectly valid business. You don't need to pretend you're reimagining anything. 'Our team is passionate about [thing nobody is passionate about].' Nobody is passionate about invoice reconciliation, Brenda. It's okay.

Every founder bio has the same structure: 'After graduating from [prestigious university], [Name] worked at [Google/Meta/McKinsey] before realizing that [industry] was broken and needed to be disrupted.' Brother, you worked at McKinsey for nine months and then your parents gave you seed money. That's also fine. Just say that.

I counted the word 'leverage' on one startup's landing page. Eleven times. ELEVEN. They leveraged AI to leverage data to leverage insights to leverage outcomes. At that point you're not leveraging anything, you're just stacking the word on top of itself like a leverage Jenga tower.

Also can we talk about the testimonials? 'This product changed everything for our team. - Sarah K., VP of Operations.' Sarah K. is the founder's girlfriend. I checked LinkedIn. She works at a dog grooming salon. A lovely salon, I'm sure, but perhaps not the enterprise validation they were going for.

I'm begging startups: just be normal. Tell me what your product does in one sentence. Show me a screenshot. Let me try it. I don't need a gradient. I don't need a manifesto. I don't need six stock photo models celebrating your API documentation.

title: Slack was supposed to replace email. Now I have Slack AND email AND Teams AND Discord AND WhatsApp groups. I am communicating more and saying less.
content:
I want to describe my morning communication routine and I need you to understand that I am not exaggerating even slightly.

7:00 AM: Wake up. Check phone. 14 unread Slack channels. 847 unread emails. 3 Teams notifications from someone named Gerald who I think works in accounting but might also be a bot. A Discord server I accidentally joined during a hackathon in 2019 that I can't figure out how to leave has 200+ new messages. And a WhatsApp group called 'Quick Sync' has 4,000 messages from overnight because half the team is in a different timezone. The word 'quick' is doing HEAVY lifting in that group name.

7:15 AM: Open Slack. My company has 847 channels. I am in 73 of them. 71 of them are either dead or indistinguishable from each other. There's #engineering and #engineering-general and #eng-team and #dev-chat and #engineering-discussions and I genuinely do not know which one to post in. Last time I picked wrong and someone DMed me 'hey that should probably go in #eng-team not #engineering-general' like I had committed a federal crime.

7:30 AM: Someone sends me an email that says 'Did you see my Slack message?' I did not. Someone sends me a Slack message that says 'I sent you an email about this.' I open the email. The email says 'Let's discuss this on Teams.' I open Teams. The Teams message says 'Actually let's take this to WhatsApp, it's easier.' I open WhatsApp. The WhatsApp message says 'Can you send me an email summary of this?' I am going to scream.

8:00 AM: I have a meeting. The meeting invite is in Google Calendar but the link is for Zoom. The meeting notes are in Notion. The action items will go into Jira. The follow-up discussion will happen in Slack. The decision will be communicated via email. By the time the information reaches its final destination, it's been through more platforms than a piece of luggage at O'Hare.

Remember when Slack launched and the whole pitch was 'where work happens' and it was going to REPLACE email? Instead it just added another layer. Every new tool that promises to simplify communication just becomes another communication channel you have to monitor. It's like trying to solve traffic by building more highways. You just get more traffic.

The absolute worst is when someone sends a message on the wrong platform and you have to play detective. 'Hey did anyone share that design doc?' 'Yeah, I think Jake posted it somewhere.' WHERE. Where did Jake post it. Was it Slack? Email? Teams? The shared Google Drive? The OTHER shared Google Drive? The Notion page? The Confluence wiki that nobody uses but technically still exists? Jake, WHERE DID YOU PUT IT.

I spend roughly 45 minutes per day just CONTEXT SWITCHING between communication tools. That's not communicating. That's just commuting between apps. I'm a digital nomad except all the destinations look like slightly different versions of the same chat interface.

We didn't simplify communication. We distributed it across nine platforms and added read receipts so everyone can see that you saw their message and chose not to respond. True innovation.
source_title: The Collaboration Tool Paradox: Workers Now Spend 4.2 Hours Daily Managing Messages

title: The tech industry's obsession with 'disruption' has led to a $4,000 internet-connected juicer that squeezes bags. Peak Silicon Valley was 2017 and we're still recovering.
content:
I think about Juicero at least once a month and every time it makes me question whether capitalism is working as intended.

For those who don't know the story, and honestly I envy you, Juicero was a startup that made a $400 machine (originally $700!) that squeezed proprietary juice bags. You could not use regular fruit. You had to buy their special bags, which contained pre-chopped fruit and vegetables. The machine had WiFi. It had a QR code scanner. It connected to your phone. It was, and I cannot stress this enough, a juice bag squeezer.

Then in 2017, Bloomberg reporters discovered you could squeeze the bags with your bare hands and get the same amount of juice in roughly the same amount of time. They posted a video. The video went viral. The company shut down four months later.

The company had raised ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY MILLION DOLLARS. $120,000,000. For a bag squeezer. The founder previously founded a raw food restaurant. The investors included Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins, which are not joke firms—these are the people who backed Amazon and Google. Nobody at any point during the funding rounds, the product development, the manufacturing, the marketing campaigns—NOBODY said 'wait, what happens if we just... squeeze the bag?'

But Juicero wasn't even the most unhinged thing to come out of that era. Let me take you on a tour of Peak Silicon Valley:

Theranos: 'What if we could do hundreds of blood tests from a single drop of blood?' (They couldn't. Literally none of it worked. The founder is in prison.)

WeWork: 'What if we leased office space and then subleased it but called it a TECH COMPANY and valued it at $47 billion?' (It was worth approximately $0 billion. The founder bought a $60 million jet with investor money.)

Quibi: 'What if we made a streaming service but all the shows are 10 minutes and you can only watch on your phone?' (They spent $1.75 billion. It lasted 6 months. Nobody watched a single show.)

Bodega: 'What if we replaced corner stores with vending machines and named the company after the stores we were trying to kill?' (The backlash was immediate and devastating. They rebranded within a week.)

And my personal favorite: a startup called Yo, which was an app that let you send the word 'Yo' to your friends. That's it. That's the entire app. One button. One word. It raised $1.5 million. ONE POINT FIVE MILLION DOLLARS. For an app that sends a two-letter word.

The pattern was always the same: take a problem that doesn't exist, or a solution that already exists and works fine, wrap it in an app with a clean UI and a sans-serif logo, write a pitch deck with the words 'disrupting a $X billion industry,' get VCs to wire eight figures, burn through it in 18 months, and then pivot or die.

The scary thing is that era didn't really end. It just rebranded. Every Juicero from 2017 is an AI wrapper in 2025. Different buzzword, same energy. 'We're using AI to disrupt the $400 billion napkin industry.' Sure you are. Show me the bag squeeze video.
source_title: The Juicero Moment: How 2017 Became Silicon Valley's Waterloo
